body: Hi @jihyerish, as you can see from the Travis CI results, the build is failing. This makes it hard to review your changes. Can you fix the patch so that it compiles and builds, at least locally on your computer? Let us know if you need any help.
You also seem to have made a lot of changes that revert recent work we've done on HTML. If you could please not do that, that would be ideal.
@domenic Sorry! I didn't know that. I'll fix this.
I had a quick question. Why don't we use the same options as ScrollIntoViewOptions in this case as well? Is there any attribute there that doesn't apply here?

@NavidZ You're right. As [ScrollIntoViewOptions](https://drafts.csswg.org/cssom-view/#dictdef-scrollintoviewoptions), the scrollOptions specifies the scrolling behavior and the scrolling position, but there is  `none` value for the scrolling behavior which makes no scrolling of an element.

From that point of view, [ScrollIntoViewOptions](https://drafts.csswg.org/cssom-view/#dictdef-scrollintoviewoptions) may have  `none` value and use it in here.

Basically that is what I was suggesting. Instead of defining a new dictionary why not just reuse the ScrollIntoViewOption which also has other applicable options like _inline_ and then somewhere add a none behavior and in the steps of the focus just call into ScrollIntoView or something. This way you don't even need to redefine all the behavior of values for the keys in ScrollIntoViewOptions.
Although I wonder whether just adding a none value to the `ScrollIntoViewOptions` or `ScrollBehavior` makes sense or not. Since when we have those dictionaries we always do want to scroll.
I wonder if it is worth doing a little future proofing here. Say we can have a dictionary here for the focus function only which has bunch of attributes regarding the focus action. One of which is `Scroll` and can be either `none` meaning no scrolling at all or can be a ScrollIntoViewOptions. This way if we want to add other behaviors regarding focus we can easily extend this dictionary with other keys. @domenic @RByers @dtapuska @jihyerish WDYT?
thank u

@domenic 
I had a question regarding the behavior of not doing the scroll. I assume when someone calls `.focus()` it is as if they called `.focus({scrollOptions: {behavior: auto}})` with us specifying default values in the IDL. Now if they want to not to scroll which one is better/correct: `.focus({scrollOptions: false})` or `.focus({scrollOptions: undefined})`

> I had a question regarding the behavior of not doing the scroll. I assume when someone calls `.focus()` it is as if they called `.focus({scrollOptions: {behavior: auto}})` with us specifying default values in the IDL. Now if they want to not to scroll which one is better/correct: `.focus({scrollOptions: false})` or `.focus({scrollOptions: undefined})`

If someone calls `.focus()`, that is always equivalent to calling `.focus({scrollOptions: undefined})`. What that does is dependent on how we spec it, but presumably we want it to be backward-compatible, so we will spec it to do no scrolling.

`.focus({scrollOptions: false})` will usually behave the same as `.focus({scrollOptions: {})`. The exception is if someone has added properties to `Boolean.prototype`; if that happens, those can impact the scroll options.

> If someone calls .focus(), that is always equivalent to calling .focus({scrollOptions: undefined}). What that does is dependent on how we spec it, but presumably we want it to be backward-compatible, so we will spec it to do no scrolling.

I was under this impression that `.focus()` is the same as `.focus(undefined)` and is different from `.focus({scrollOptions: undefined})`. Am I wrong?
Anyhow, my understanding is that currently calling `focus() `will scroll to the element. At least as far as I tested unless there are some weird scenarios. If that is true so `focus()` with no parameter should scroll (and if this is the same as `.focus({scrollOptions: undefined})`) what is the best option for indicating no scrolling in FocusOptions without adding the `none` to the `ScrollBehavior`?

My only concern for adding the "none" to ScrollBehavior is that it is a parameter to a function that its job is to scroll with different behaviors. So if one doesn't want to scroll they shouldn't even call into that function (i.e. scrollIntoView) in the first place rather than a parameter telling that function to do nothing. However, that was the only thing I had in mind which I agree it might not be the strongest point. So if we cannot come up with anything clean I certainly would be fine with adding `none` to `ScrollBehavior` as well.

One question regarding your suggestion:

> el.focus({ scroll: "smooth", scrollOptions: { block: "start", inline: "end" });

Isn't `scrollOptions`'s type `ScrollIntoViewOptions` already? Which means it has an attribute `behavior` to specify `ScrollBehavior` (e.g.  "auto", "instant", "smooth"). So what does `scroll` represent in your example?

My point was that we should not worry about the IDL; we should figure out what user-facing API we want. Thus this may involve creating new enumerations, dictionaries, or any of that so as to get the better experience for users. I'd like us to figure out what that experience is, before worrying about how it fits with existing or new IDL constructs.

How about this:
`.focus()` (To be same as `.focus({scrollOptions: {block:'center', inline:'center', behavior: 'auto'}})` or whatever right now the default behavior precisely is for compat.
`.focus({scrollOptions: false})` or `.focus({scrollOptions: {}})` -> Does no scrolling
`.focus({scrollOptions: {block:X, inline:Y, behavior: Z}})` -> Does whatever X,Y,Z imply.

Hmm, that departs from JavaScript APIs in several ways that we should avoid:

- It mixes types: sometimes `focusOptions` is a boolean, sometimes an object. Typically we do not allow such mixing in our APIs; booleans (either true or false) get treated as an empty object.
- It treats `{}` as something other than "fill in the default values". In general, passing an empty options object should be the same as passing an options object with all its defaults filled in.

Can we come up with an API that avoids these pitfalls?

I tried to mimic the same pattern as what we have in [ScrollIntoView](https://www.w3.org/TR/cssom-view-1/#extension-to-the-element-interface) in which they check the argument type and if it is object they do one thing and if it is boolean they do something else. So can I assume that is because that's an old API and it was only for compat reasons that is designed like that?
Yeah, exactly.

That seems like a reasonable API design, although I'd quibble on the naming (just `scroll` instead of `scrollEnabled`).

It does seem a bit unfortunate for users compared to my version, in that

```js
el.focus({ scroll: true, scrollOptions: { behavior: "smooth" } });
```

seems unnecessarily verbose compared to

```js
el.focus({ scroll: "smooth" });
```

What is your motivation for the more-verbose version?
So in your version what happend to scrollOptions. Does that exist? I mean can someone pass that as well?
Yep, that was in my last example. It only contains block and inline members, though.
But if the type of that is ScrollIntoViewOptions that already has that `behavior` option there. Doesn't  it? So how do we differentiate between those two options?

If you're asking how we implement the desired API in IDL, after agreeing on it being the desired API, that's simple: we define a new dictionary type.

I don't understand the "differentiate" comment though.

I see. So your `scrollOptions` isn't `ScrollIntoViewOptions`. It is a new dictionary. So you are suggesting to re-define all the attributes and their enums that are related to scrolling once again in focus and always keep them sync with the ones defined in the [scrolling](https://www.w3.org/TR/cssom-view-1/#extension-to-the-element-interface)?
How about making `focus` take a `ScrollIntoViewOptions` dictionary. If it's passed we scroll using those options. If it's null we don't?

> So you are suggesting to re-define all the attributes and their enums that are related to scrolling once again in focus and always keep them sync with the ones defined in the [scrolling](https://www.w3.org/TR/cssom-view-1/#extension-to-the-element-interface)?

Not the enums or attributes, just a dictionary with two members (block and inline). Do you anticipate this being hard to keep in sync?

> How about making `focus` take a `ScrollIntoViewOptions` dictionary.

That was discussed up at https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2787#issuecomment-311388719 and rejected as that prevents future expansion to other non-scroll-related options.

> If it's passed we scroll using those options. If it's null we don't?

That doesn't work in Web IDL/JavaScript API design, where `null` (or `undefined`) trigger the default behavior (which in this case is scrolling). See https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2787#issuecomment-315938733

> Not the enums or attributes, just a dictionary with two members (block and inline). Do you anticipate this being hard to keep in sync?

I don't know. It just doesn't feel right to have them defined again here.

If the problem is only with the lengthy notation can we have the `scroll` attribute to be true by default (which also matches the `.focus()`). So when it is not passed it is considered true and then if you like to change the scrolling behavior you can also pass `scrollOptions` Does this match with JavaScript API design to consider not specified and true to behave the same and false by itself as something else?

I don't think we should be concerned about what feels right for spec factoring, but instead about what feels right for users of the API. If Web IDL had some construct (e.g. "[dictionary mixins](https://github.com/heycam/webidl/issues/195)") which allowed us to deduplicate the spec definition, then presumably it would not longer feel wrong to you. But the end-user API would be exactly the same. To me it sounds like we are thus constraining ourselves based on our tools, not based on what's best for users.

We cannot have the scroll attribute be true by default, no; [booleans must default to false](https://w3ctag.github.io/design-principles/#prefer-dict-to-bool). In fact, it sounds like your proposal would be backward-incompatible, because it would change the default to not scrolling. We could get around that by changing the name of the boolean, e.g. `avoidScroll: true`. But that seems even less user-friendly.

@domenic 
> We cannot have the scroll attribute be true by default, no; booleans must default to false. In fact, it sounds like your proposal would be backward-incompatible, because it would change the default to not scrolling. We could get around that by changing the name of the boolean, e.g. avoidScroll: true. But that seems even less user-friendly.

I again was mimicking from [scrolling](https://www.w3.org/TR/cssom-view-1/#extension-to-the-element-interface) which I guess I should stop doing it :). They have a clause saying "If arg is not specified or is true, ...".

How about `preventScroll` instead of `avoidScroll`? "prevent" is more often used like in preventDefault and stuff like that. Does it still give the double negation feeling if one sets the `preventScroll` to `false` which will be the default value?

@jihyerish 

> Am I understanding right?

Yeah. You are correct.
@domenic has concerns about the name of that scrollEnabled and the default value in my proposal. On the other hand, I have concerns about adding "none" to `ScrollBehavior` since one can then call element.ScrollIntoView({behavior: 'none'}) in the APIs and expect to do nothing which makes it somewhat a funny API.

> "future expansion to other non-scroll-related options" is about adding "none" to the ScrollBehavior?

That means we can add anything else that we may want in the future (I don't know what that could be at the moment) to the `FocusOptions` without touching `ScrollIntoViewOptions`. If you remember at first the plan was that focus function to only get a `ScrollIntoViewOptions` like this:
`.focus(ScrollViewIntoOptions option)` instead of `.focus(FocusOptions option)`.  That would have prevented us from adding any focus only related option to the focus function as we couldn't have added them to ScrollIntoViewOptions.

I'm pretty convinced at this point that we should not reuse ScrollIntoViewOptions, since it was designed to retrofit itself into a legacy API. I still haven't heard any compelling argument against my proposed API, from the perspective of users.

> I'm pretty convinced at this point that we should not reuse ScrollIntoViewOptions, since it was designed to retrofit itself into a legacy API. 

I didn't quite get this statement? What is wrong with ScrolIntoViewOptions? It has all attributes related to doing the scroll action and nothing else.

> I still haven't heard any compelling argument against my proposed API, from the perspective of users.

I assume you are saying that we should add "none" to ScrollBehavior enum. Right? Then do you agree that if someone calls Element.ScrollIntoView({behavior:"none"}) that function should do nothing?

> The only objections I've seen to this so far have been on code-structuring grounds (i.e. unease with duplication). But none of them have been on usability grounds. The duplication is relatively easy to fix, with no web-visible changes, via changes to Web IDL (e.g. dictionary mixins; enum inheritance). But an API with poor usability is not easy to fix, and has bad consequences for our users.

Yeah. We can definitely ignore how we prevent the duplications in the Web IDL front as you said it can be solved with bunch of other constructs. I can see that `ScrollIntoViewOptions` is used in an old legacy API and that API got some modifications to be able to use this dictionary but I don't see the reason that you are pulling the properties of `ScrollIntoViewOptions` out of it and breaking it into different constructs.

What you are doing here is restructuring the scrolling options here. `ScrolIntoViewOptions` by itself seems to be a complete and well designed dictionary to contain all the scrolling related attributes. So if the user agent wants to scroll an element into view having a dictionary of type `ScrolIntoViewOptions` is necessary and sufficient to know how exactly to do the scroll. Do you agree with me so far?

If you agree with the previous paragraph, from the developer's perspective if there is one place in my app defining how the scrolling should be done across my app I expect the construct that defines this to be unique across all the APIs of the platform so I can reuse the same thing again instead of restructuring it for different APIs.
To make the matter a little worse, imagine this scenario here. Say we land this patch. Now tomorrow there will be another API `Element.foo()` which it **may** need to focus the element depending on what user passes to `foo()`. As we currently have `.focus()` always focuses an element and that is not what `foo` needs. How do you think they need to define their API and let the caller to disable/enable the focus? If they do similar to what you are suggesting they would break up the FocusOptions into the attributes of FooOptions and not use FocusOptions at all in anyway in their parameters. Doesn't that sound weird from the users of that API? Isn't this what we are doing with ScrollIntoViewOptions?

> Do you agree with me so far?

I agree with the framing that if you know you want to scroll, ScrollIntoViewOptions is a reasonable way to customize that.

However, the options were designed for an API that always scrolls. They are not a good fit for situations where you are not sure whether or not you are going to scroll. It needs another supplementary signal to figure that out.

The issue then is that it seems to me more natural to merge this signal into scroll behavior. That is, instead of a 2x3 matrix of { scroll yes, scroll no } x { auto, instant, smooth }, we should just have four choices: { scroll no, scroll auto, scroll instant, scroll smooth }.

We also have an issue with focus() in particular where we need to scroll by default. Thus, any on/off signal must default to on. But that doesn't work with booleans, so we need to go with a double-negative, e.g. `preventScroll: true` / `preventScroll: false`. Merging it into a spectrum of scroll behaviors sidesteps this issue. And in general, introducing such a spectrum of scroll behaviors (including "none") is something we can reuse throughout the platform.

> from the developer's perspective if there is one place in my app defining how the scrolling should be done across my app I expect the construct that defines this to be unique across all the APIs of the platform so I can reuse the same thing again instead of restructuring it for different APIs.

This is a great argument! Perhaps this kind of reuse makes it worth the awkwardness and verbosity compared to my API. I'm not sure myself; it still feels like we're letting one API with legacy constraints prevent us from using a better API throughout. That is, we're going from one API design for scrollIntoView(), and turning it into two, and thus the next N. I'd rather we call the scrollIntoView() design legacy, create a better pattern that's more applicable, and use that for the next N.

> To make the matter a little worse, imagine this scenario here.

The answer seems simple to me: they'd just define a version of FocusOptions with a different default for the scroll member. In IDL terms, this indeed may look like breaking things out into FooOptions and not using FocusOptions. But that's just a spec-writing detail. For developers, they still get a good API.

For ScrollIntoViewOptions, we don't have that luxury of reusing it in that way, because it's not designed as a general scroll options API: it's only suitable for APIs where you're always scrolling.

> The answer seems simple to me: they'd just define a version of FocusOptions with a different default for the scroll member. In IDL terms, this indeed may look like breaking things out into FooOptions and not using FocusOptions. But that's just a spec-writing detail. For developers, they still get a good API.

I wasn't talking about optional scrolling for the foo API. I was talking about optional focusing in the foo API.
I can see your argument for `ScrollIntoView` being legacy is based on the fact that `ScrollIntoView` always does the scroll. So now that in `focus` we may or may not want to scroll we need to something about it.
At the same time, in `foo` may or may not want to do the **focus** and focus function always does focus. Now there is no field in `FocusOptions` to disable focus. So `foo` can not modify any default value or anything in `FocusOptions` to achieve that.

I see.

After a day to noodle on things, and combined with your earlier argument about potentially reusing the scrollOptions across multiple APIs, I am no longer convinced that my proposal is significantly better. Thanks for taking the time to get me there. Special apologies to @jihyerish, whose first contribution became a large multi-day back-and-forth!

I still think we don't have a lot of nice options here. But, we'll do what we can. By my accounting we have two main possibilities:

- Add "none" to ScrollBehavior in CSSOM; then the API is `focus({ scroll })`, where `scroll` is the updated `ScrollIntoViewOptions`. CSSOM can be defined to either throw or ignore `"none"`, treating it like an invalid value like it currently does, or it can have `scrollIntoView()` be a no-op when given `behavior: "none"`.

- Add a `preventScroll` boolean option; then the API is `focus({ preventScroll, scrollOptions })`, where `scrollOptions` is the current `ScrollIntoViewOptions`. `scrollOptions` is ignored if `preventScroll` is true.

Does this sound right? I don't have a real preference between these two, and am happy to let you, @jihyerish, and @bokand champion whichever you prefer. I'm also open to exploring other ideas.

Seems like we're making a tradeoff:

The first option makes ScrollIntoViewOptions more general at the cost of allowing some contradictory combinations (i.e. `scrollIntoView({behavior: "none"})` ). The upside is this fits into more APIs and you can use just one dictionary to specify a wider range of behavior.

The second option avoids dealing with contradicting instructions but I think it requires being slightly more verbose. To confirm my understanding, in this case, we'd have a nested dictionary, right? i.e. `focus({ preventScroll: false, scrollOptions:{behavior: "smooth"}})`

I was partial to the second option but after thinking about it some more I think `scrollIntoView({behavior: "none"})` makes sense even if it's a bit unintuitive/useless and avoiding nested dictionaries would be nice. So I also don't feel strongly and am fine with either choice.

Chatted offline with @NavidZ and he convinced me that the second option is preferable on two points:

- We'd still have a nested dictionary in the first case so we're not actually improving the form (since using ScrollIntoViewOptions directly would make additions to the focus() API difficult)
- By adding a "none" scroll behavior, we'd be restricting future APIs that use ScrollIntoViewOptions since we can't design a new, rational API that always scrolls. It would have to handle the "none" option.

Just want to make sure everyone has the same information, still OK with either one...

> The first option makes ScrollIntoViewOptions more general at the cost of allowing some contradictory combinations (i.e. `scrollIntoView({behavior: "none"})` )

It depends on what you mean by allow. Right now that throws a TypeError [per Web IDL](https://heycam.github.io/webidl/#es-enumeration). We could make it throw a TypeError in the CSSOM spec, and then there would be no difference from before.

> By adding a "none" scroll behavior, we'd be restricting future APIs that use ScrollIntoViewOptions since we can't design a new, rational API that always scrolls. It would have to handle the "none" option.

Again, we can just have such future APIs throw when given "none".

> Add "none" to ScrollBehavior in CSSOM; then the API is focus({ scroll }), where scroll is the updated ScrollIntoViewOptions. CSSOM can be defined to either throw or ignore "none", treating it like an invalid value like it currently does, or it can have scrollIntoView() be a no-op when given behavior: "none".
> 
> Add a preventScroll boolean option; then the API is focus({ preventScroll, scrollOptions }), where scrollOptions is the current ScrollIntoViewOptions. scrollOptions is ignored if preventScroll is true.
> 

Between above possibilities, I prefer the first idea for the following reasons: 

- There are several enums which have "none" value or similar one("disabled") such as:
enum [TextTrackMode](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#texttrackmode) { "disabled",  "hidden",  "showing" };
enum [PremultiplyAlpha](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#premultiplyalpha) { "none", "premultiply", "default" };
- For the second idea, it feels like focus() will have too much parameters just for scrolling. Currently most browsers scroll the focused element into view if it is outside of the view with 'instant' scroll behavior. Also in general, using the "none" scrolling is a rare case. So I think having a boolean parameter (preventScroll) isn't a good design for the focus().
- If "none" is added to [ScrollIntoViewOptions](https://drafts.csswg.org/cssom-view/#dictdef-scrollintoviewoptions), it may be also useful for [scrollIntoView()](https://drafts.csswg.org/cssom-view/#dom-element-scrollintoview). 
For example, after we call [scrollIntoView()](https://drafts.csswg.org/cssom-view/#dom-element-scrollintoview) to an element, and if the element is transitioned from visibility:visible to visibility:hidden, we can see that the hidden element still makes scrolling.
See the sample here: https://jsfiddle.net/JihyeHong/cu5ad0qh/

> Again, we can just have such future APIs throw when given "none".

Yup, though I would argue that an API that throws on invalid inputs is worse than one that doesn't allow an invalid combination to be specified. Though it may be preferable to alternatives.

> If "none" is added to ScrollIntoViewOptions, it may be also useful for scrollIntoView().
For example, after we call scrollIntoView() to an element, and if the element is transitioned from visibility:visible to visibility:hidden, we can see that the hidden element still makes scrolling.
See the sample here: https://jsfiddle.net/JihyeHong/cu5ad0qh/

I'm not sure I understand how "none" helps in this case. If you don't want scrollIntoView() to show a hidden element, wouldn't you just avoid calling it, rather than changing it's behavior parameter to "none"? Or am I misunderstanding?

What do you mean by "doesn't allow"? Because the Boolean-including proposal doesn't allow invalid inputs... by throwing when they are provided. (Remember, there is no compile time checking here; all errors are runtime errors.)
You're right, I'm coming at this from a strict-compiled language perspective - feel free to disregard me :)

So, I'm not terribly well-versed in the various OM APIs, but since @jihyerish asked for my opinion, there's a couple things I recommend to keep in mind:
  * First, whatever this API ends up being, it should be as consistent as possible with other scrolling-related APIs like scrollIntoView, scrollTo, scrollBy, etc. (And therefore probably also warrants review by the groups in charge of those APIs in addition to the semi-random group of individuals that happen to be paying attention here, but in any case questions like what to do with invalid arguments should be resolved the same way by all related APIs.)
  * Second, as for the preferred position of the focused element, the [CSS Scroll Snap module](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-scroll-snap/) already defines various parameters for the preferred scroll positions for viewing an element, and imho it is better to re-use these rather than establish a contradictory and less powerful set of arguments in the .focus() API. The `scroll-padding` property already specifies that it applies, and probably `scroll-snap-margin` should as well. The spec currently avoids specifying that focusing operations inherently trigger snapping to the element’s snap position, but it does specify that (even when snapping is off), a #fragmentID-targetted element should snap into position... so if this is desired behavior we can look into defining that behavior as well. In any case, it doesn't seem like this belongs specifically in the JS API, unless for some reason the behavior of an API call needs to differ from that of a user-triggered event.
The proposal above looks good to me

> Thanks to the opinion from @fantasai and discussion with @anawhj, I came up with the IDL like this:

That doesn't seem to work because it makes things very confusing if we add non-scroll related options to focus. E.g., let's consider if we later added `speak` for some kind of audio announcement of scrolling. Then the code

```js
el.focus({ speak: true, behavior: "smooth" });
```

would be confusing, because you think it's talking about a smooth speaking behavior, but actually it's just talking about scrolling behavior. That's why earlier in the thread, in the last paragraph of https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2787#issuecomment-311388719, @NavidZ pointed out that we need to go with a nested dictionary.

So if we're not interested in adding `"none"` to ScrollBehavior, we should go with option 2 from https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2787#issuecomment-317121142.

I also really don't understand why people say that adding a value to an enum that is not accepted by all APIs taking the enum is not appropriate or proper. If the API doesn't accept the value, that's the same (in JavaScript) as it not existing in the first place. I'm worried that people are making decisions based on misunderstanding how JavaScript API design works, if this is their criteria.

> In the discussion with @jihyerish, we can hit on an additional idea about a way to simply handle no scrolling. 

This is interesting. However it's not as simple as "adding preventScroll", nor is it a minimal change. We need to find all the event types relevant---so far you have identified FocusEvent and KeyboardEvent---and add a method preventScroll() to them. We then need to define the behavior of preventScroll. For example, if it is called asynchronously, is it a no-op? Does it throw an error? Or maybe, if we're halfway through scrolling, it aborts the scrolling? Etc. Still, it might be worth pursuing!
Yes, that looks perfect!

>> To support focus() behavior that makes no scrolling, we can define a new API(method) named preventScroll(). 
>
> This is interesting. However it's not as simple as "adding preventScroll", nor is it a minimal change. 

Yes, it is. An idea about preventScroll() deals with more general scrolling than focus-based scrolling, so we'll  discuss this in another thread.

@bokand @NavidZ Are you okay with [the IDL](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2787#issuecomment-319241234) like above?
@domenic @NavidZ @bokand I updated the PR reflecting the latest version of IDL. Could you review the changes?
Looks good to me but I'll defer to @NavidZ for final judgement since I'm only tangentially involved.

Is the scrollOptions taking the default value of ScrollIntoViewOptions? 
ScrollIntoViewOption has default value of block="center" and inlinePosition="center".  But current focus() is not scroll to center for all the cases. 
Chrome/Safari scroll to center when the element is not visible, do scrolling in y-axis to make element align to the edge when it's partially visible. (The behavior is kind of complicate and interesting...)
Firefox/Edge scroll to edge when visible and not scroll when partially visible.

I'm also wondering should partially visible element scroll or not? Anyone have idea about that?
I submitted a new round of review, for some reason it's hidden behind "Show outdated" above.

@EiraGe 
> Is the scrollOptions taking the default value of ScrollIntoViewOptions?

Yes, the` scrollOptions` is `ScrollIntoViewOptions`.

> ScrollIntoViewOption has default value of block="center" and inlinePosition="center". But current focus() is not scroll to center for all the cases.

You're right. Currently the scrolling triggered by focus() is not specced, so the scrolling works differently for browsers. So if this PR is merged, I think it can also help with that problem. : )

> I'm also wondering should partially visible element scroll or not? Anyone have idea about that?

By default the partially visible element scrolls into the view. 
You can see the related discussion in here: https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2787#discussion_r124345739
Thanks @zcorpan ! :scream: Sorry about that.   Maybe that's my mistake.

> ScrollIntoViewOption has default value of block="center" and inlinePosition="center".

This will likely also change, per https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/1720

> But current focus() is not scroll to center for all the cases.

> You're right. Currently the scrolling triggered by focus() is not specced, so the scrolling works differently for browsers. So if this PR is merged, I think it can also help with that problem. : )

So the question here is, what do browsers want to converge towards? Maybe the defaults for `focus()` should be different from those of `scrollIntoView()`? Certainly they behave differently in browsers now; specifying something else, without clear support from implementors, isn't going to work.
Can someone post the latest IDL or point out how to see it in the pull request?
@othermaciej You can see the latest IDL here : https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2787#issuecomment-319241234.
@zcorpan @domenic I updated the PR. Could you review the changes?

@jihyerish Thanks! It seems odd that this uses nested dictionaries. Is that a common pattern? CSSOM itself has the ScrollIntoViewOptions dictionary inherit from a base ScrollOptions dictionary instead of embedding it, so fewer braces needed. I noticed the dictionary nesting in various versions of the IDL in this thread and it was never explained, so maybe there's a good reason for it that I'm just not familiar with.
@othermaciej see https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2787#issuecomment-319081118 for rationale.

As noted in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2787#issuecomment-324864085 I think the main issue remaining is the defaults. What is specified here doesn't match any browser, does it?

The defaults for `ScrollIntoViewOptions` will likely change per https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/1720

Maybe `scrollOptions` should be a different dictionary with different defaults (like nearest-nearest?).

So I think there are a few possibilities to move forward.
